'''Miriam Yevick''' ({{Nee|Lipschutz}}; August 28, 1924 — September 5, 2018) was an American [[mathematician]] and professor at [[Rutgers University College]]. She was the fifth woman to receive a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] from [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in math. She immigrated to the United States with her family after fleeing [[German-occupied Europe|Nazi Belgium]] in 1940. She is known for her collaboration with [[David Bohm]] on his [[Quantum physics|quantum theories]].

== Education and early life ==
Yevick was born in [[Scheveningen]] to prominent [[Diamonds as an investment|diamond merchant]] Max Lipschutz.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |date=2018-09-18 |title=Obituaries 9/19/18 – Town Topics |url=https://www.towntopics.com/2018/09/18/42743/ |access-date=2025-12-03 |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-09-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250912070705/https://www.towntopics.com/2018/09/18/42743/ |url-status=live }}</ref> She was of Jewish descent.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |date=October 16, 1996 |title=USC Shoah Foundation Institute testimony of Miriam Yevick |url=https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/vha21052 |website=The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum |access-date=January 1, 2026 |archive-date=October 14, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251014220421/https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/vha21052 |url-status=live }}</ref> She attended [[Montessori education|Montessori]] school in [[the Hague]], after which time her family relocated to [[Belgium]] where she attended [[Collège Marie-José (Antwerp)|Collège Marie-José]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite thesis |last=Yevick |first=Miriam Amalie Lipschutz |title=The lebesgue density theorem in abstract measure spaces |date=1947 |degree=Thesis |publisher=Massachusetts Institute of Technology |url=https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/85715 |archive-date=2025-10-17 |access-date=2026-01-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251017085958/https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/85715 |url-status=live }}</ref> When she was 16, they immigrated to the [[United States]] in 1940 from [[Antwerp]],<ref name=":5" /> fleeing the [[German-occupied Europe|Nazi regime]] and was a survivor of [[The Holocaust]].<ref name=":4" /> The escape took three months.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Lipschutz Yevick |first=Miriam |title=A Testament for Ariela |publisher=Blue Thread |year=2012 |isbn=9780985113803}}</ref> She graduated from [[Lycée Français de New York]] in 1942.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |title=AALFNY: In Memoriam |url=https://www.lfnyalumni.org/en/news/no.36/50/2115/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241110074416/https://www.lfnyalumni.org/en/news/no.36/50/2115/ |archive-date=2024-11-10 |access-date=2025-12-03 |website=www.lfnyalumni.org}}</ref>

She received her [[Bachelor of Arts]] from [[New York University]] in 1943. She then enrolled at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) where she earned a [[Master of Science]] in [[Physics]] in 1945,<ref name=":0" /> and in 1947 she became the fifth woman in history to receive a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] in [[Mathematics]] from MIT.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2012-11-09 |title=Guest lecturer, author recalls flight from fascism, shares life lessons |url=https://www.clarku.edu/news/2012/11/09/guest-lecturer-author-recalls-flight-from-fascism-shares-life-lessons/ |access-date=2025-12-03 |website=ClarkU News |language=en-US}}</ref> While at MIT, she met her husband, physicist [[George Yevick]]. Their son, [[David Yevick|David]], and granddaughter, [[Hannah Yevick|Hannah]], are also physicists.<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Yevick |first=David |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/book/10.1002/9781118979792 |title=Fundamental Math and Physics for Scientists and Engineers |last2=Yevick |first2=Hannah |date= |publisher=Wiley |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-470-40784-4 |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.1002/9781118979792}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Yevick began her career at the [[National Bureau of Standards]] in [[Washington, D.C.]],<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|pages=|page=79}} shortly after she met [[David Bohm]] in 1948,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Freire Junior |first=Olival |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-030-22715-9 |title=David Bohm: A Life Dedicated to Understanding the Quantum World |date=2019 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-22714-2 |series=Springer Biographies |location=Cham |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-22715-9}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=|page=113}} at which time they began an affair.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|pages=79–80}} Yevick and her husband remained in close contact with Bohm, and corresponded with him while he was at [[University of São Paulo]] on his [[De Broglie–Bohm theory|causal interpretation of quantum theory]]. Bohm requested from Yevick a [[mathematical proof]] to support a statistical mechanics argument that rare exceptions are negligible, such that typical behavior could be treated as physically reliable.<ref>{{Citation |last=Talbot |first=Chris |chapter=Single Pages of Letters to Miriam Yevick and Letter to George Yevick |date=2017 |title=David Bohm: Causality and Chance, Letters to Three Women |pages=437–446 |editor-last=Talbot |editor-first=Chris |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-319-55492-1_33 |access-date=2026-01-01 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-55492-1_33 |isbn=978-3-319-55491-4|chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Peat |first=F. David |title=Infinite potential: the life and times of David Bohm |date=1997 |publisher=Addison Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-40635-1 |series=Helix books |location=Reading, Mass}}</ref> On Bohm's [[holonomic brain theory]], Yevick postulated that the brain has the capacity to process [[waveform]]s with a [[Fourier analysis|Fourier logic]].<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9781134914173 |title=Quantum Implications: Essays in Honour of David Bohm |date=2012-06-25 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-203-39279-9 |editor-last=Hiley |editor-first=Basil |edition=0 |language=en |doi=10.4324/9780203392799 |editor-last2=Peat |editor-first2=F. David}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=481–482}}

She held visiting posts at the [[University of Victoria]], [[Princeton University]], and [[City College of New York]].<ref name=":8">{{Cite web |last=Benzon |first=William |date=2023-10-09 |title=Next year in Jerusalem: The brilliant ideas and radiant legacy of Miriam Lipschutz Yevick [in relation to current AI debates] - 3 Quarks Daily |url=https://3quarksdaily.com/3quarksdaily/2023/10/next-year-in-jerusalem-the-brilliant-ideas-and-radiant-legacy-of-miriam-lipschutz-yevick-in-relation-to-current-ai-debates.html |access-date=2025-12-03 |language=en-US}}</ref> In 1964,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lipschutz-Yevick |first=Miriam |date=2007 |title=Poetic metaphor and mathematical demonstration: A shallow analogy |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02985683 |journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer |language=en |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=11–13 |doi=10.1007/BF02985683 |issn=0343-6993|url-access=subscription }}</ref> she was appointed to a professorship at [[Rutgers University College]], where she spent the rest of her career teaching [[Remedial education|remedial math]] until she retired.<ref name=":8" />

On her work ''Holographic or fourier logic'' (1975),<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lipschutz Yevick |first=Miriam |date=1975 |title=Holographic or fourier logic |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0031320375900059 |journal=Pattern Recognition |language=en |volume=7 |issue=4 |pages=197–213 |doi=10.1016/0031-3203(75)90005-9 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2024-11-01 |access-date=2026-01-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20241101233808/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0031320375900059 |url-status=live }}</ref> cognitive scientists William Benzon and [[David G. Hays]] formulated 'Yevick's Law' in 1988.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Benzon |first=W |date=1988 |title=Principles and development of natural intelligence |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0140175088900619 |journal=Journal of Social and Biological Systems |language=en |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=293–322 |doi=10.1016/0140-1750(88)90061-9 |url-access=subscription |archive-date=2024-04-14 |access-date=2026-01-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240414064039/https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0140175088900619 |url-status=live |last2=Hays|first2=David G.}}</ref> Benzon later wrote that Miriam's work provides a foundational framework for understanding [[intelligence]]. He argues that her work shows how intelligence depends on choosing between modes of [[Symbolic artificial intelligence|symbolic]] or [[Holography|holographic]] computation and that systems of [[artificial intelligence]] struggle to balance them.<ref name=":9">{{Cite web |last=Benzon |first=William |date=2023-10-09 |title=Next year in Jerusalem: The brilliant ideas and radiant legacy of Miriam Lipschutz Yevick [in relation to current AI debates] - 3 Quarks Daily |url=https://3quarksdaily.com/3quarksdaily/2023/10/next-year-in-jerusalem-the-brilliant-ideas-and-radiant-legacy-of-miriam-lipschutz-yevick-in-relation-to-current-ai-debates.html |access-date=2025-12-03 |language=en-US |archive-date=2025-10-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251005225203/https://3quarksdaily.com/3quarksdaily/2023/10/next-year-in-jerusalem-the-brilliant-ideas-and-radiant-legacy-of-miriam-lipschutz-yevick-in-relation-to-current-ai-debates.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Benzon |first=William L. |title=What Miriam Yevick Saw: The Nature of Intelligence and the Prospects for A.I., A Dialog with Claude 3.5 Sonnet |date=2025 |url=https://www.ssrn.com/abstract=5081013 |access-date=2025-12-03 |doi=10.2139/ssrn.5081013}}</ref>

In 2012, she published a memoir in the form of letters she had written to her first grandchild,<ref name=":9" /> ''A Testament for Ariela'', about her life escaping from a Nazi regime to become a mathematician.<ref name=":7" /><ref name=":6" />
